cards.title: Conditional probability
cards.what:
- **Restrict** the world to B, then ask how much of it is A.

$$P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$$
cards.what_full:
P(A | B) is the probability of A once you know B happened. Knowing B shrinks the sample space to B alone.

Take a fair die. B = "even" = {2, 4, 6}. A = "at least 4" = {4, 5, 6}.

Only 4 and 6 are in both. So P(A and B) = 2/6 and P(B) = 3/6.

$$P(A\mid B)=\frac{2/6}{3/6}=\frac{2}{3}$$

The division rescales: B is now the whole world, so its probability must become 1.
cards.why:
- Core of **GATE DA** probability questions.
- It unlocks **Bayes**, then naive Bayes in ML.
cards.why_full:
Almost every probability question in the paper conditions on something: a test result, a draw already made, a column already chosen.

It also builds toward the chain rule, independence, Bayes' theorem, and later naive Bayes and graphical models in ML.
how: Count or compute the **overlap** with A.
how_full: Name the given event B, the thing you already know. It goes after the bar.
Find P(A and B). Use a table, a tree, or counting.
Divide by P(B). This rescales so that B has probability 1.
Sanity check: the answer must be between 0 and 1, and at most 1 if A contains B.
cards.trap: Don't flip the bar. **P(A|B)** is not P(B|A). Ask which event is given.
cards.trap_full:
People read P(A|B) as "chance of B given A" because they read the letters left to right.

Example: most cricketers are fit, but most fit people are not cricketers. P(fit | cricketer) is high; P(cricketer | fit) is tiny.

cards.title: Bayes' theorem
cards.what:
- **Flip** a conditional: from P(+|D) to P(D|+).

$$P(D\mid +)=\frac{P(+\mid D)\,P(D)}{P(+)}$$
cards.what_full:
Bayes' theorem turns "how likely is this evidence if the cause is true" into "how likely is the cause given this evidence".

It comes from writing P(D and +) in two ways: P(+ | D) P(D) and P(D | +) P(+). Set them equal and divide by P(+).

The denominator P(+) is found by adding every way a + can happen (total probability):

$$P(+)=P(+\mid D)P(D)+P(+\mid \neg D)P(\neg D)$$
cards.why:
- **Medical test** and spam-filter questions are Bayes questions.
- It unlocks the **naive Bayes** classifier in ML.
cards.why_full:
GATE DA uses Bayes in screening-test, defective-item and two-urn questions: you know how the evidence behaves, and you want the cause.

In ML, naive Bayes classifies by computing P(class | features) with exactly this formula, plus an independence assumption.
how: Draw the **tree**: cause first, evidence second.
how_full: Draw a tree. First split by cause (sick or healthy), with the prior on each edge. Reason: priors are what you know before the test.
Second split by evidence (+ or -), with the likelihood on each edge. Reason: these are the test's error rates.
Multiply along each full path. Example: 0.01 x 0.95 = 0.0095. A path product is the probability of that whole story.
Cross out paths that contradict what you observed (here, the negative ones).
Posterior = target path / sum of surviving paths = 0.0095 / (0.0095 + 0.0495) = 0.161.
cards.trap: Don't read **95% accurate** as a 95% chance of disease. The prior matters.
cards.trap_full:
The test catches 95% of sick people, but only 1% of people are sick. The 99% healthy produce 5% false positives, which is far more people than the true positives.

So most positives are false alarms, and P(D | +) is only about 16%. A rare cause needs strong evidence.

cards.title: Prior and posterior
cards.what:
- **Prior** is what you believe before evidence.
- **Posterior** is the updated belief after it.
cards.why: - Names the **inputs and output** of every Bayes question.
cards.trap: Don't skip the base rate. A tiny prior drags the posterior down.

steps.caption: Start with the prior. Only 1 person in 100 has the disease D. The other 99 do not.
Now everyone is tested. A sick person tests positive 95% of the time. A healthy person tests positive 5% of the time (a false positive).
Multiply along a branch to get the chance of the whole path. Sick and positive: 0.01 x 0.95 = 0.0095.
Healthy and positive: 0.99 x 0.05 = 0.0495. This is the bigger number, because healthy people are so many.
We are told the test came back positive. So negative branches cannot have happened. Remove them. Only the two + paths remain.
Posterior = the sick-and-positive path divided by all positive paths. A positive test gives only about a 16% chance of disease.
